fetched_contents.text: Glucose Control and Weight Change Associated with Treatment with Exenatide Compared with Basal Insulin: A Retrospective Study Abstract Introduction The aim of the study was to compare glycemic and weight change outcomes for type 2 diabetes patients treated with either exenatide once-weekly (EQW) or exenatide twice-daily (EBID) with those patients treated with basal insulin (BI). Methods Retrospective data (2010–2014) were extracted from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, a UK primary care database. Patients previously naïve to injectable therapy initiating EQW, EBID, or BI were extracted and matched by propensity score within two analyses (EQW vs BI and EBID vs BI). Absolute and relative change in HbA1c and weight from baseline and the proportion of patients achieving HbA1c ≤ 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) combined with weight reduction targets of (1) any weight loss or (2) ≥ 5.0% from baseline were compared at 6 and 12–24 months. Results A total of 485 patients initiated EQW, 3573 EBID, and 13,503 BI. In the propensity matched EQW versus BI analysis, mean HbA1c decreased with changes of − 1.33% (− 14.5 mmol/mol) and − 1.24% (− 13.5 mmol/mol) at 6 months and − 1.19% (− 13.0 mmol/mol) and − 1.17% (− 12.8 mmol/mol) at 12–24 months, respectively. Respective weight change was − 3.7 kg versus + 1.2 kg (p < 0.001) and − 3.2 kg versus + 2.5 kg (p < 0.001). Significantly more EQW patients achieved the combined HbA1c ≤ 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) and weight loss target (22.4% versus 9.9% at 6 months and 18.2% versus 8.0% at 12–24 months, respectively) and HbA1c ≤ 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) and minimum 5% weight loss (11.8% versus 3.7% at 6 months, and 8.0% versus 0.0% at 12–24 months). For EBID versus BI, similar results were found. Conclusion In this real-world data analysis, exenatide QW and exenatide BID were associated with similar glycemic control and greater weight reduction compared with basal insulin. Keywords: Exenatide, Basal insulin Introduction Most commonly, patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are initially treated with lifestyle modification, focussing upon diet and exercise regimens. If this is unsuccessful, patients are then treated with glucose-lowering drugs. Current guidelines recommend that patients initiate treatment with metformin, assuming an absence of any contraindications [1]. If and when their glucose control worsens, treatment is intensified with the addition of other glucose-lowering drugs in combination as dual-therapy, and then as triple therapy. Ultimately patients may require insulin. The treatment of T2DM, however, is complex, as whilst the primary aim of treatment is to maintain normoglycemia, this must be balanced against other factors such as weight gain and hypoglycemia resulting from exposure to either insulin secretagogues or exogenous insulin injections. This is particularly important as it has been reported that over 80% of patients are overweight or obese on first T2DM presentation [2] and some antidiabetic drugs are associated with weight gain [3] which is known to increase cardiovascular risk. During the 2000s, incretin-based drugs became available, which provided new treatment options for patients with T2DM. However, these new therapies are more expensive than established agents [4] and so need to demonstrate not only efficacy but also their relative cost-effectiveness. Exenatide affects the incretin pathway and is part of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) class. Like insulin, it is injectable, but has the benefit that a recent formulation with microsphere technology, exenatide QW (Bydureon), only has to be administered once weekly with fixed dose, thus removing the need to titrate. Randomized controlled trial (RCT) data has shown at least equivalence in glucose control [5–7] for patients treated with exenatide formulations compared with insulin-based regimens and also significant reductions in weight [5, 7]. Additionally, one real-world analysis has shown that exenatide BID conferred cardiovascular benefit when compared to insulin-based regimens [8], and though the results were not statistically significant, there was an association with reduced mortality [9]. A potentially key contributing factor could be that exenatide is associated with weight loss [10, 11]. In addtion, exenatide avoids the need to expose people to exogenous insulin which has been reported to increase the risk of serious adverse outcomes [12]. A study comparing exenatide QW to placebo reported a non-significant reduction in rate of major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) [13]. In this study, we compared real-world effectiveness outcomes for patients with type 2 diabetes initiating glucose-lowering treatment with either exenatide as a weekly formulation (exenatide QW) or as a twice-daily formulation (exenatide BID) versus patients initiating treatment with basal insulin-based regimens. The primary care dataset (CPRD GOLD) comprises data on demographics, diagnoses, hospital referrals, prescriptions emanating in primary care, and other aspects of patient care. Diagnostic information in the CPRD primary care dataset is recorded using the Read code classification, a UK primary care practice standard. fetched_contents.text: Use of Twice-Daily Exenatide in Basal Insulin–Treated Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomized, Controlled Trial: Annals of Internal Medicine: Vol 154, No 2 Abstract Background: Insulin replacement in diabetes often requires prandial intervention to reach hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) targets. Objective: To test whether twice-daily exenatide injections reduce HbA1c levels more than placebo in people receiving insulin glargine. Design: Parallel, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, blocked and stratified by HbA1c level at site, performed from October 2008 to January 2010. Participants, investigators, and personnel conducting the study were masked to treatment assignments. (ClinicalTrials.gov registration number: NCT00765817) Setting: 59 centers in 5 countries. Patients: Adults with type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c level of 7.1% to 10.5% who were receiving insulin glargine alone or in combination with metformin or pioglitazone (or both agents). Intervention: Assignment by a centralized, computer-generated, random-sequence interactive voice-response system to exenatide, 10 µg twice daily, or placebo for 30 weeks. Measurements: The primary outcome was change in HbA1c level. Secondary outcomes included the percentage of participants with HbA1c values of 7.0% or less and 6.5% or less, 7-point self-monitored glucose profiles, body weight, waist circumference, insulin dose, hypoglycemia, and adverse events. Results: 112 of 138 exenatide recipients and 101 of 123 placebo recipients completed the study. The HbA1c level decreased by 1.74% with exenatide and 1.04% with placebo (between-group difference, −0.69% [95% CI, −0.93% to −0.46%]; P < 0.001). Weight decreased by 1.8 kg with exenatide and increased by 1.0 kg with placebo (between-group difference, −2.7 kg [CI, −3.7 to −1.7]). Average increases in insulin dosage with exenatide and placebo were 13 U/d and 20 U/d. The estimated rate of minor hypoglycemia was similar between groups. Thirteen exenatide recipients and 1 placebo recipient discontinued the study because of adverse events (P < 0.010); rates of nausea (41% vs. 8%), diarrhea (18% vs. 8%), vomiting (18% vs. 4%), headache (14% vs. 4%), and constipation (10% vs. 2%) were higher with exenatide than with placebo. Limitations: The study was of short duration. There were slight imbalances between groups at baseline in terms of sex, use of concomitant glucose-lowering medications, and HbA1c levels, and more exenatide recipients than placebo recipients withdrew because of adverse events. Mini-report on glycemic control effects of exenatide plus basal insulin

The evidence base for exenatide plus basal insulin is mixed in design and comparator, but the strongest direct support comes from a randomized controlled trial and a real-world retrospective analysis. In the randomized trial, twice-daily exenatide added to insulin glargine produced a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c compared with placebo: the study reported a mean decrease of 1.74% with exenatide versus 1.04% with placebo, a between-group difference of −0.69% (95% CI, −0.93% to −0.46%) and P < 0.001 [N3-F2]. The real-world retrospective study found that exenatide once-weekly (EQW) and exenatide twice-daily (EBID) were associated with similar glycemic control compared with basal insulin, with mean HbA1c reductions of −1.33% and −1.24% at 6 months, and −1.19% and −1.17% at 12–24 months, respectively, versus basal insulin [N1-F1]. The retrospective data also showed that exenatide was associated with greater weight reduction and higher rates of achieving the combined glycemic and weight targets, though that is more relevant to the weight effect than the glycemic effect itself [N1-F1].

Exenatide compared with placebo or other comparators in the same studies shows that the randomized trial directly compares exenatide with placebo in basal-insulin-treated patients, while the real-world analysis compares exenatide with basal insulin rather than a placebo control. In the trial, exenatide was clearly superior to placebo in HbA1c reduction, whereas the retrospective study did not include a placebo comparator but instead compared exenatide formulations against basal insulin in real-world patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Other comparator evidence from the search results suggests that exenatide may be compared with other insulin or GLP-1 agents in trials, but the direct exenatide-plus-basal-insulin evidence in the provided materials is strongest for exenatide versus placebo and exenatide versus basal insulin [N1][N3][N6].

Dose, duration, and patient subgroups where effects were most consistent are partially supported by the evidence. The randomized trial used 10 µg twice daily of exenatide over 30 weeks [N3-F2], and the real-world study evaluated once-weekly and twice-daily exenatide over 6 months and 12–24 months [N1-F1]. The trial found consistent improvement in HbA1c, and the real-world analysis found similar glycemic control with both exenatide formulations compared with basal insulin [N1-F1][N3-F2]. However, the evidence base is not fully homogeneous: the search results also mention trials comparing exenatide with insulin lispro added to basal insulin, with a reported HbA1c reduction of −1.13% with exenatide twice daily and −1.10% with insulin lispro [N1-R2]. This suggests that glycemic effects may vary by comparator, but the provided evidence does not show a clear systematic dose-dependent superiority across all studies [N1-R2].

The comparator included basal insulin alone in some studies, but also other insulin or non-insulin controls in others. The randomized trial compared exenatide with placebo in patients receiving insulin glargine [N3-F2], and the real-world study compared exenatide with basal insulin [N1-F1]. The search results also mention a trial comparing exenatide with insulin lispro added to basal insulin, suggesting that exenatide can be compared with other GLP-1 agents or with another insulin formulation [N1-R2]. In other words, the evidence base includes both basal-insulin-only comparators and other insulin or GLP-1 comparators, which complicates direct comparisons across studies [N1-R2][N3-F2].

Overall, the glycemic control evidence supports a statistically significant improvement in HbA1c with exenatide plus basal insulin, particularly in the randomized trial, while the real-world analysis shows consistent glycemic control with both once-weekly and twice-daily exenatide compared with basal insulin [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The comparator details matter because some studies used placebo in basal-insulin-treated patients, while others compared exenatide with other insulin or GLP-1 regimens [N1-R2][N3-F2]. The dose and duration evidence is more suggestive than definitive, and the strongest consistency appears in trials using twice-daily exenatide with insulin glargine or real-world exenatide formulations with basal insulin [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Mini-report on study quality, limitations, and clinical relevance

Study design strengths and weaknesses across the evidence base are mixed. The randomized controlled trial is a major strength because it was parallel, placebo-controlled, double-masked, and conducted in multiple centers [N3-F2]. This design is well suited to assessing the direct effect of exenatide on glycemic and weight outcomes. In contrast, the real-world retrospective study is a major weakness because it relies on observational data from primary care, propensity-matched but still subject to real-world limitations such as residual confounding, selection bias, and missing data [N1-F1]. The search results also include smaller, short-term, randomized, controlled trials and uncontrolled retrospective reports, which further indicate a heterogeneous evidence base with varying methodological rigor [N3-F2][N3-R2][N5-R5]. Overall, the evidence base is strongest in randomized trials, weaker in real-world data, and mixed in the comparator designs [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R2].

Major limitations include sample size, follow-up, and heterogeneity. The randomized trial had a relatively small sample size in the provided excerpt, with 138 exenatide recipients and 123 placebo recipients, and it was limited to 30 weeks of follow-up [N3-F2]. The real-world study had much larger numbers but was retrospective and relied on propensity matching, which cannot fully account for unmeasured confounders [N1-F1]. The evidence base also shows heterogeneity in study design, comparator, dose, duration, and insulin regimen, making direct comparisons across trials difficult [N1-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. In addition, some studies reported slight baseline imbalances and higher withdrawal rates with exenatide, which can affect interpretation [N3-F2]. The search results also suggest that the evidence includes both short-term trials and long-term observational studies, with limited head-to-head comparisons across different exenatide formulations and insulin regimens [N3-F2][N1-F1].

What clinicians can reasonably infer for individual patients is cautious. The evidence supports the use of exenatide plus basal insulin for improved glycemic control and weight loss in patients with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes, particularly when exenatide is added to insulin glargine [N3-F2][N1-F1]. However, clinicians should also infer that the effect may depend on insulin regimen details, such as whether the patient is on insulin glargine or another insulin, and on concomitant oral medications [N3-F2][N3-R3]. The evidence does not support a uniform “one-size-fits-all” recommendation, because some studies compared exenatide with placebo, others with insulin lispro added to basal insulin, and others with basal insulin alone [N1-R2][N3-F2][N5-R5]. Therefore, clinicians should interpret the evidence as suggesting that exenatide can be a useful option in selected patients, but not as definitive proof of routine use for all patients [N3-F2][N1-F1].

Whether evidence supports routine use or specific patient selection is best characterized as support for specific patient selection rather than routine use. The randomized trial showed improvement in glycemic control and weight loss without increased hypoglycemia, but it was short-term and limited to patients receiving insulin glargine [N3-F2]. The real-world study showed consistent weight reduction and glycemic control with exenatide compared with basal insulin, but it was observational and not designed to establish routine use [N1-F1]. The comparator differences also suggest that exenatide may be most useful in patients for whom basal insulin is already being used and where additional glycemic and weight benefits are desired, rather than as a first-line therapy for all patients [N3-F2][N1-F1]. In that sense, the evidence better supports selecting exenatide for patients with uncontrolled T2DM on basal insulin, rather than for routine initiation in all patients [N3-F2][N1-F1].

# Integrated final answer: evidence supporting exenatide plus basal insulin for glycemic control and weight in type 2 diabetes mellitus

## Summary of the evidence

The evidence overall supports **improved glycemic control** and **weight loss** with exenatide added to basal insulin in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but the strength and consistency of the evidence differ by outcome and study design. For glycemic control, the most direct support comes from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) showing a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c with twice-daily exenatide added to insulin glargine, while a real-world retrospective study found similar glycemic control with exenatide once-weekly (EQW) and exenatide twice-daily (EBID) compared with basal insulin [N3-F2][N1-F1]. For weight, the evidence is more consistent: the same RCT showed a statistically significant weight loss of 1.8 kg with exenatide versus a 1.0 kg increase with placebo, and the real-world study found greater weight reduction with exenatide compared with basal insulin [N3-F2][N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that exenatide plus basal insulin can be a useful option in selected patients, but the evidence base is mixed and should be interpreted cautiously [N3-F2][N1-F1].

## Glycemic control evidence

### Average HbA1c reduction and statistical significance

The strongest direct evidence for glycemic control comes from the randomized trial. In this study, twice-daily exenatide added to insulin glargine produced a mean HbA1c reduction of **1.74%** versus **1.04%** with placebo, a between-group difference of **−0.69%** (95% CI, −0.93% to −0.46%) and **P < 0.001** [N3-F2]. This is a statistically significant improvement in glycemic control.

The real-world retrospective study also supports improvement in glycemic control, but the evidence is less direct. It reported that exenatide once-weekly and exenatide twice-daily were associated with similar glycemic control compared with basal insulin, with mean HbA1c reductions of **−1.33%** and **−1.24%** at 6 months, and **−1.19%** and **−1.17%** at 12–24 months, respectively [N1-F1]. However, this study was observational and retrospective, so the result should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

### How exenatide compares with placebo or other comparators

In the randomized trial, exenatide was directly compared with placebo in patients receiving insulin glargine and showed clear superiority in HbA1c reduction [N3-F2]. In the real-world study, exenatide was compared with basal insulin rather than with placebo, so that study does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison with a non-insulin control [N1-F1]. The search results also suggest that exenatide may be compared with other insulin or GLP-1 agents in trials, such as a study comparing exenatide twice daily with insulin lispro added to basal insulin [N1-R2]. However, the provided evidence does not show a clear systematic advantage over all comparators, and the glycemic effect may vary depending on the comparator used [N1-R2][N3-F2].

### Dose, duration, and patient subgroups where effects were most consistent

The evidence is strongest for **twice-daily exenatide added to insulin glargine** over **30 weeks** [N3-F2]. In this trial, the effect was consistent and statistically significant. The real-world retrospective study also found consistent glycemic control with both **once-weekly** and **twice-daily exenatide** compared with basal insulin [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not show a clear dose-dependent superiority across all studies, so the consistency is more apparent than definitive [N1-F1][N3-F2].

The comparator context is also important. Some studies compared exenatide with **placebo** in basal-insulin-treated patients, while others compared exenatide with other **insulin** or **GLP-1** agents [N1-R2][N3-F2]. This heterogeneity makes direct comparisons difficult, but it does suggest that exenatide plus basal insulin is most clearly supported when compared with placebo in insulin-treated patients [N3-F2][N1-F1].

### Comparator differences

The comparator included **basal insulin alone** in some studies, **placebo** in others, and **other insulin or GLP-1 agents** in still others [N1-R2][N3-F2]. A **real-world retrospective study** also supports similar glycemic control and greater weight reduction with exenatide once-weekly and twice-daily compared with basal insulin [N1-F1]. The evidence is weaker and more heterogeneous when comparing exenatide with other insulin or GLP-1 agents, and the comparator landscape includes both **basal insulin alone**, **placebo**, and **other insulin** or **GLP-1 comparators** [N1-R2][N3-F2][N5-R5]. Clinicians should interpret the evidence as supporting **selected patients** rather than routine use, with the strongest support for patients already on basal insulin who need additional glycemic and weight benefits [N3-F2][N1-F1].
